title: India-Born Scientist Shankar Balasubramanian Wins 2026 Wolf Chemistry Prize
excerpt: The Cambridge chemist shares the award with David Klenerman and Pascal Mayer for the DNA-sequencing technology that cut the cost of reading a human genome from over $1 billion to about $1,000.
body:
• India-born chemist Shankar Balasubramanian has won the 2026 Wolf Prize in Chemistry, announced October 1 by the Wolf Foundation at the President's Residence in Jerusalem.
  • He shares the prize with David Klenerman of Cambridge and Pascal Mayer of France for the sequencing chemistry behind Solexa/Illumina, the platform that made large-scale, low-cost DNA reading practical.
  • Balasubramanian and Klenerman already hold the 2020 Millennium Technology Prize and the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences; Chemistry World tips them as future Nobel contenders.
  • For Indian students and researchers: the award is a reminder that careers in fundamental science produce world-scale impact — the pair's chemistry now underpins more than a million human genome sequences a year.

India-born scientist Shankar Balasubramanian has won the 2026 Wolf Prize in Chemistry, one of the world's most prestigious science honors, for the DNA-sequencing technology that turned reading a human genome into a routine, thousand-dollar procedure.

The Wolf Foundation announced the laureates on October 1 at the President's Residence in Jerusalem. The awards will be presented in June 2027.

The prize and the discovery

Balasubramanian shares the chemistry prize with David Klenerman, his colleague at the University of Cambridge, and Pascal Mayer of France. The foundation cited complementary contributions that together made next-generation sequencing practical: Balasubramanian and Klenerman developed the sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry — fluorescently labeled bases with temporary blocks, read cycle by cycle by a camera — and co-founded the company Solexa to commercialize it. Mayer conceived the DNA-colony amplification method that boosts each fragment's signal so it can be read.

https://x.com/ERC_Research/status/2105985849066492131

The impact is hard to overstate. When the first human genome was sequenced in 2000, it took more than a decade and cost over a billion dollars. Today, thanks to the technology the laureates developed, a human genome can be sequenced in a single day for about $1,000, and more than a million human genomes are sequenced at scale each year, according to the University of Cambridge. The platform powers cancer care, genetic diagnosis, infectious-disease tracking, and biological research worldwide.

The Wolf Prize, awarded in Israel since 1978, carries a $100,000 award and a reputation as a precursor to the Nobel — many past laureates have gone on to win in Stockholm. With this year's Nobel announcements due, Chemistry World has already tipped Balasubramanian and Klenerman as its top 2026 chemistry contenders.

Who Balasubramanian is

Born in India, Balasubramanian is a professor in Cambridge's Yusuf Hamied Department of Chemistry, a researcher at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute, and a Fellow of Trinity College. Along with Klenerman, he co-invented the Solexa sequencing method and co-founded Solexa, whose technology became the dominant genome-sequencing platform after its acquisition by Illumina.

The Wolf Prize is the latest in a run of top honors. The pair won the 2020 Millennium Technology Prize — one of the world's largest technology awards — and the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences. Accepting the Millennium Prize, Balasubramanian said:

"I am absolutely delighted at being awarded the Millennium Technology Prize jointly with David Klenerman, but it's not just for us, I'm happy on behalf of everyone who has contributed to this work."

— Shankar Balasubramanian, on winning the 2020 Millennium Technology Prize

The other 2026 laureates

In medicine, the prize went to Charles S. Zucker of Columbia University and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, for research that transformed the understanding of taste — identifying the sensory cells and receptors for sweet, sour, bitter, salty, and umami, and mapping the neural pathways that carry the signals from tongue to brain.

The physics prize was shared by Immanuel Bloch of the Max Planck Institute and the University of Munich, for using ultracold atoms trapped in light lattices to simulate complex quantum systems, and Jun Ye of the University of Colorado and the National Institute of Standards and Technology, for developing optical atomic clocks of extraordinary precision.

A diaspora pattern at the Wolf Prize

The award continues a run of Indian-diaspora laureates at the Wolf Prize. Last year, Indian American physicist Jainendra Jain of Pennsylvania State University won the 2025 Wolf Prize in Physics for his prediction of composite fermions, a new class of quantum particles. Two straight years of diaspora winners at one of science's top honors is a measure of how deeply Indian-origin researchers are embedded in the world's leading laboratories.

What's next

The formal award ceremony takes place in June 2027 in Israel. Before that, all eyes are on the Nobel announcements: a Wolf Prize in the same year has historically strengthened laureates' cases in Stockholm, and Balasubramanian and Klenerman have been on chemistry prediction lists for years.
